title: Outliers III - Percentile Method and Winsorization
abstract:
The third and fourth detection techniques from the notes. The percentile method
abandons distributional assumptions entirely: you simply decide a minimum and
maximum percentile threshold and treat everything outside as an outlier.
Winsorization is the capping version of the same idea. This document defines
percentiles precisely, shows how the method differs from trimming, derives the
effect on the mean and variance, gives the guidance on choosing the threshold,
and closes with the full comparison of all four outlier techniques.

blocks.t: Percentiles
From the notes

items: E.g. 99% means 99% of people are behind me.
If the maximum value is 95, then that is the 100th percentile.
Decide a min & max percentile threshold.
Capping using percentile is called Winsorization.

blocks.cap:
A percentile is a rank expressed as a percentage. The curve is the
 empirical CDF: read a value on the $x$-axis and the curve tells you what
 fraction of the data lies at or below it.

blocks.t: Definition
The $p$th percentile of a sample is the value $v_p$ such that
P(X \le v_p) = \frac{p}{100}.

Equivalently it is the inverse of the empirical CDF, $v_p = F^{-1}(p/100)$.
Special cases you already know:
The interpolation detail

With $n$ data points, most percentiles fall between two observations, so
the value must be interpolated. numpy defaults to linear interpolation;
pandas matches it. Other conventions exist ("nearest",
"lower", "midpoint"), which is why two libraries can report
slightly different percentiles for the same data. It rarely matters, but it
explains discrepancies.
The Percentile Method
The whole method

Decide a minimum and maximum percentile threshold. Anything below the
lower one or above the upper one is an outlier. That is all — there is no
formula to derive and no distribution to assume.
Typical choices: 1st/99th, 2.5th/97.5th, 5th/95th.
The distinguishing property

Z-score and IQR compute how many rows will be flagged — you specify a
rule and the data decides the count. The percentile method specifies the
count — you choose 1% per tail and you get exactly 1% per tail, on any
distribution whatsoever.
That is either its great strength or its great weakness:

items:
Strength: completely distribution-free. Works identically on
 normal, skewed, bimodal and heavy-tailed data. You control the cost.

Weakness: it flags 1% even when the data is perfectly
 clean. The method has no notion of "there are no outliers here".

blocks.t: Winsorization
From the notes
Capping using percentile is called Winsorization.

Named after Charles Winsor. Instead of deleting the extreme rows, replace each
one with the threshold value:

blocks.cap:
The same column, three ways. Trimming removes rows and shrinks $n$.
 Winsorization keeps every row and produces a visible spike exactly at the cap
 — that spike is the cost of the method, and it is the signature that tells a
 reviewer you winsorized.

head: Trimming (percentile)
Winsorization
rows: Replace them with the threshold value
The extreme values are real but too influential

blocks.t: Effect on the moments

Let $F$ be the distribution and $v_p$, $v_{1-p}$ the thresholds. The winsorized
mean is
\mu_W = p v_p + \int_{v_p}^{v_{1-p}} x dF(x) + p v_{1-p}.
Two consequences:

items:
On a symmetric distribution, $\mu_W = \mu$ — the two tails
 cancel, and winsorization gives an unbiased but lower-variance estimate of
 the centre.

On a skewed distribution, $\mu_W \neq \mu$. Winsorizing income
 deliberately biases the mean downward. If a business metric depends
 on total income, you have changed the answer.

blocks.t:
The winsorized variance is always smaller than the true variance, and this is the
point: the estimator's breakdown point rises from 0% to $p$.
Do not winsorize the target if the total matters

Capping a feature bounds its influence on the model — usually desirable. Capping
the target changes what the model is predicting. If you cap claim amounts
at the 99th percentile and then use the model to forecast total payouts, you will
systematically under-forecast, because the real tail is where most of the money
is. Cap features freely; think hard before capping targets.
Choosing the Threshold

blocks.cap:
Left: the mean and standard deviation as a function of how much you
 cap — the choice is a real modelling decision, not a formality. Right: the
 four techniques on the same column, showing how differently they behave.

head: Threshold
When
rows: Very large datasets; you only want to remove clear data errors
Heavy contamination, or a small dataset where a few points dominate
The right choice for a one-sided variable. Income has no meaningful left tail, so cap only the right

blocks.t: Asymmetric thresholds are usually correct

Nothing requires the two tails to be treated equally. For any quantity with a
natural floor — income, price, duration, count — there is no left tail to
speak of, and capping at the 1st percentile removes real low values for no
reason. Set the lower threshold to 0 and cap only the right.
Treat it as a hyperparameter

The percentile is a number you choose, which makes it exactly the kind of thing
cross-validation should decide. Put the capper in a pipeline and search over
thresholds against the downstream metric — that replaces an argument about
"how much is too much" with evidence.

blocks.t: Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from scipy.stats.mstats import winsorize
from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, GridSearchCV, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
income = np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.3, .6, 3000), rng.uniform(300, 900, 25)]

# =====================================================================
# 1. PERCENTILES -- the definitions from the notes
# =====================================================================
print("50th percentile:", np.percentile(income, 50).round(2))
print("median         :", np.median(income).round(2), " <- the same thing")
print("100th percentile:", np.percentile(income, 100).round(2))
print("maximum         :", income.max().round(2), " <- the same thing")

# "99% means 99% of people are behind me"
v99 = np.percentile(income, 99)
print(f"\n99th percentile = {v99:.2f}")
print(f"fraction of the data at or below it: {np.mean(income <= v99):.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE PERCENTILE METHOD -- decide a min and max threshold
# =====================================================================
LOWER_PCT, UPPER_PCT = 1, 99
lo, hi = np.percentile(income, [LOWER_PCT, UPPER_PCT])
outlier = (income < lo) | (income > hi)

print(f"\nthresholds: [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]")
print(f"flagged: {outlier.sum()} rows ({outlier.mean():.2%})")
# EXACTLY 2% -- because you asked for 1% per tail. The data had no say.

# THE DISTINGUISHING PROPERTY: it flags 2% even on perfectly clean data
clean = rng.normal(50, 10, 5000)
a, b = np.percentile(clean, [1, 99])
print(f"on CLEAN normal data, percentile flags {np.mean((clean<a)|(clean>b)):.2%}")
print(f"                      z-score    flags "
      f"{np.mean(np.abs(clean-clean.mean())>3*clean.std()):.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 3. TRIMMING vs WINSORIZATION
# =====================================================================
trimmed = income[~outlier]                       # rows DELETED
wins    = np.clip(income, lo, hi)                # rows KEPT, values capped

print(f"\n{'':14s} {'n':>6s} {'mean':>9s} {'std':>9s} {'skew':>7s} {'max':>9s}")
for name, v in [("original", income), ("trimmed", trimmed), ("winsorized", wins)]:
    print(f"{name:14s} {len(v):6d} {v.mean():9.2f} {v.std():9.2f} "
          f"{stats.skew(v):7.2f} {v.max():9.2f}")

print(f"\nvalues changed by winsorizing: {int((wins != income).sum())}")
print(f"rows sitting exactly at the cap: {int((wins == hi).sum())}  <- the spike")

# scipy has it built in (note: limits are FRACTIONS, not percents)
sp = np.asarray(winsorize(income, limits=[0.01, 0.01]))
print("matches scipy:", np.allclose(np.sort(sp), np.sort(wins)))

# pandas one-liner:
s = pd.Series(income)
print("pandas clip:", np.allclose(s.clip(*s.quantile([.01, .99])).values, wins))

# =====================================================================
# 4. THE EFFECT ON THE MEAN -- symmetric vs skewed
# =====================================================================
sym = rng.normal(100, 15, 20_000)
skw = rng.lognormal(3.3, .8, 20_000)
for name, v in [("symmetric", sym), ("skewed", skw)]:
    a, b = np.percentile(v, [1, 99])
    w = np.clip(v, a, b)
    print(f"{name:10s} mean {v.mean():9.2f} -> winsorized {w.mean():9.2f}  "
          f"({(w.mean()-v.mean())/v.mean():+.2%})")
# Symmetric: the two tails cancel, the mean barely moves.
# Skewed:    the mean is pulled DOWN. You have deliberately biased it.

# =====================================================================
# 5. ASYMMETRIC THRESHOLDS -- usually the correct choice
# =====================================================================
# income has a natural floor; there is no meaningful left tail to cap
lo_sym, hi_sym = np.percentile(income, [1, 99])
lo_asym, hi_asym = income.min(), np.percentile(income, 99)
print(f"\nsymmetric 1/99 removes {np.mean(income < lo_sym):.2%} from the left "
      f"-- real low incomes, deleted for no reason")
print(f"asymmetric 0/99 removes 0% from the left, "
      f"{np.mean(income > hi_asym):.2%} from the right")

# =====================================================================
# 6. ALL FOUR TECHNIQUES ON THE SAME COLUMN
# =====================================================================
m, sd = income.mean(), income.std()
q1, q3 = np.percentile(income, [25, 75]); iqr = q3 - q1
techniques = {
    "z-score 3sigma": (m - 3*sd,          m + 3*sd),
    "IQR 1.5":        (q1 - 1.5*iqr,      q3 + 1.5*iqr),
    "percentile 1-99":  tuple(np.percentile(income, [1, 99])),
    "percentile 5-95":  tuple(np.percentile(income, [5, 95])),
}
print(f"\n{'technique':18s} {'lower':>9s} {'upper':>9s} {'flagged':>9s}")
for name, (a, b) in techniques.items():
    print(f"{name:18s} {a:9.2f} {b:9.2f} {np.mean((income<a)|(income>b)):9.2%}")

# =====================================================================
# 7. AS A PIPELINE TRANSFORMER, WITH THE THRESHOLD TUNED
# =====================================================================
class PercentileCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
    """Winsorize at the given percentiles. Thresholds LEARNED from train."""
    def __init__(self, lower=1.0, upper=99.0):
        self.lower, self.upper = lower, upper

    def fit(self, X, y=None):
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        self.lower_ = np.nanpercentile(X, self.lower, axis=0)
        self.upper_ = np.nanpercentile(X, self.upper, axis=0)
        return self

    def transform(self, X):
        return np.clip(np.asarray(X, dtype=float), self.lower_, self.upper_)

    def get_feature_names_out(self, input_features=None):
        return np.asarray(input_features, dtype=object)

n = 4000
X = np.c_[np.r_[rng.lognormal(3.2, .6, n-25), rng.uniform(300, 900, 25)],
          rng.normal(35, 8, n)]
y = (0.03*np.clip(X[:, 0], 0, 90) + 0.05*X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 1, n) > 3.4).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

for name, steps in [
    ("none",           [("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("winsorize 1/99", [("cap", PercentileCapper(1, 99)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("winsorize 5/95", [("cap", PercentileCapper(5, 95)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
    ("right tail only",[("cap", PercentileCapper(0, 99)),  ("sc", StandardScaler())]),
]:
    pipe = Pipeline(steps + [("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])
    print(f"{name:17s} cv auc "
          f"{cross_val_score(pipe, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring='roc_auc').mean():.4f}")

# The threshold is a hyperparameter -- let the data choose it
gs = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("cap", PercentileCapper()), ("sc", StandardScaler()),
              ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))]),
    {"cap__lower": [0, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5], "cap__upper": [95, 97.5, 99, 99.5, 100]},
    cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print("\nbest thresholds:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))

capper = PercentileCapper(1, 99).fit(X_tr)
print("thresholds learned from TRAIN:", capper.upper_.round(2))
# Applied UNCHANGED to test and to production. A test value above the
# training 99th percentile is capped to the TRAINING threshold -- correct,
# because that is the boundary the model was fitted under.

Step 1 – choose the caps. Take the 5th and 95th percentiles (linear interpolation):
Step 2 – clip. Values below $1.45$ become $1.45$; values above $59.05$ become $59.05$:

Step 3 – what changed. The value $100$ was replaced by $59.05$. Nothing was deleted, so the row count stays at 10. The mean drops from $145/10 = 14.5$ to $104.5/10 = 10.45$, showing how much a single extreme value was driving the average.

When to use it. Capping keeps the row (useful when the other columns in that row are informative) and limits the damage of the outlier on weight-based models such as linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. What is winsorization?

Capping using percentiles: values below the $p$th percentile are set to the $p$th
percentile and values above the $(100-p)$th are set to that. It keeps every row,
unlike trimming, and bounds the influence of extreme values while preserving the
ordering.
Q. How does the percentile method differ from the IQR method?

The IQR method derives its boundaries from the data's own spread, so the number
of flagged rows depends on the distribution. The percentile method fixes the
flagged fraction in advance — 1% per tail means exactly 1% per tail, always.
That makes it distribution-free but also means it flags rows even when the data
is clean.
Q. When is winsorization the wrong choice?

When the extreme values are the signal — fraud, defects, catastrophic claims —
and when the target's total matters. Capping claim amounts at the 99th percentile
and then forecasting total payouts systematically under-forecasts, because the
tail is where the money is.
Q. Should you always cap both tails equally?

No. For a variable with a natural floor — income, price, duration, counts —
there is no meaningful left tail, and capping at the 1st percentile deletes real
low values for no reason. Use an asymmetric threshold: 0 on the left, 99 on the
right.
Q. How do you choose the percentile threshold?

Treat it as a hyperparameter. Put the capper in a pipeline and grid-search the
thresholds against the downstream metric. Start from 1/99 as a default and let
cross-validation adjust it.

Q. Your model sees a production value above the training 99th percentile.
What happens?

It is capped to the training threshold, because that is the fitted
parameter. This is correct — the model was estimated under that boundary — but
it means the model cannot distinguish "slightly above the cap" from "far above
the cap". If that distinction matters, keep a was_capped indicator
alongside.
